slides.title: The HT16K33 and Its Device Driver
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 10 — In-Class

slides.title: Where we are
items: On Thursday you put an oscilloscope on two wires and watched a transaction go by: START, address, ACK, data, STOP.
Today the chip at the other end. Its datasheet is four pages of command table and RAM map, and by the end of the hour those pages are three functions your program can call.
That layer — the device driver — is the one this course has been handing you all term as uart.c and adc.c. This is the one you write.
By the end of the hour your own display shows ES.28, written out of a ten-byte buffer by a function you wrote. Lab 5 asks for that function.

slides.title: Finish the driver and show ES.28
Nothing on the display? Work down the layers
Recap
items: 34 LEDs on 14 wires, because a grid saves wires and a sweep buys back the one digit at a time it costs you. The backpack runs that sweep so your program does not have to.
A device's commands come out of its datasheet's command table, one byte each, and the header's names are that table's structure.
Two bytes per digit position, five positions, and the odd bytes are what advance the HT16K33's pointer — which is why they have to be sent.
All ten in ONE transaction, because a STOP ends the write and the next one starts over.
A device driver reaches the hardware only through the interface driver. SevenSeg.c may call i2c1_byteWrite() as often as it likes and may not touch I2C1->CR2 once.
Tonight: the counters. The MM:SS clock is the one that makes you find the colon bit, and Lab 5 is the same shape.
